description: Introduces the social and political contexts of archaeological research in heritage and human rights arenas, with emphasis on ethics and the law.

title: PaleoParents: The Evolution of Human Families
description: Families are fundamental to our identities as people but also something that is easily recognizable in other animals. What happened in our evolution that shaped how humans form families?

title: Human Nature: Who are we? And how did we get this way?
description: Is there such a thing as human nature? And if there is, how would we recognize it when we see it? Human nature takes an interdisciplinary approach to understanding why humans are the way we are.

description: Study of primate biocultural variation across time and space. Using an evolutionary perspective, this course explores the foundational concepts, methods, and theories used by biological anthropologists to understand living and extinct humans and non-human primates.

title: The Science of Our Past: An Introduction to Archaeology
description: Covers how and why archaeologists study evidence of past human behavior. Required labs emphasize hands-on analyses of artifacts and other archaeological materials.

title: Health, Healing, and Ethics: Cross-Cultural Perspectives on Sickness and Society
description: A cross-cultural exploration of cultures and organization of medical systems, economic development and the global exportation of biomedicine, and ethical dilemmas associated with medical technologies and global disparities in health.

title: Monkeys and Apes: The Nonhuman Primates
description: Introduces the study of nonhuman primates, from prosimians to the great apes. Explores questions of taxonomy, aspects of social behavior, and patterns of communication.

title: Self, Culture, and Mind: Introduction to Psychological Anthropology
description: Examines the interplay of culture, mind, and self in various Western and non-Western societies. Cognition, emotion, altered states, “brain sciences,” and mental health and illness are analyzed in a cross-cultural perspective.

title: North American Archaeology
description: North America’s human past, from the earliest colonization by ice age peoples and their descendants who colonized the continent, to the clash of cultures that followed the arrival of Europeans in 1492.

title: Introduction to Medical Anthropology
description: Provides an overview of methods and topics in medical anthropology, an interdisciplinary field that explores health, illness, and systems of healing through holistic and cross-cultural study. Case studies from a diversity of human societies and cultures around the globe are used to challenge assumptions of student understanding. Offers several University Curriculum components, gives students a robust introduction to this specialized subfield within Anthropology, and addresses many of the foundational concepts on the MCAT.

title: Evolutionary Approaches to Health and Disease
description: The evolutionary history of our species is used increasingly in modern medicine to understand the genetic roots of illness.

title: Ancient Disease and Human Evolution
description: An anthropological examination of ancient disease using archaeological, skeletal, historical, and biomolecular evidence, to explore how epidemics and pathogens shaped human evolution, societies, and modern health challenges.

title: Gender, Sex, and Sexuality: Global Perspectives
description: Cross-cultural and historical comparison of the life experiences of women and men in the areas of family, marriage and kinship, economic and political participation, sexuality, reproduction, ritual, and religion.

title: Mesoamerican Archaeology
description: Examines development of civilizations from village life to the great empires of Mexico. How civilizations begin, grow, change, and collapse.

title: South America: Culture, Environment, History
description: Surveys Indigenous and post-colonial perspectives on South America with a specific focus on the peoples and cultures of the Amazon. Students draw on a combination of archaeological, historical, and ethnographic evidence to examine the co-production and transformation of South American peoples and environments over time. Topics include the social organization and political economy of pre-Columbian societies, continuities and discontinuities with colonial patters of labor exploitation and socio-ecological change, and the role of politics and economics in framing regional social dynamics today.

title: Peoples of Africa
description: A contemporary study of the cultures and social structures of sub-Saharan African peoples and an examination of the dynamics of contemporary African societies.

title: Origins of Civilization
description: Considers those cultural and historic factors that led to the development of agriculture and the first urban states in Egypt and Mesopotamia.

title: People and Cultures of Southeast Asia
description: Introduces students to selected theoretical and ethnographic topics in the anthropological study of Southeast Asia including the geography, history, people, and cultures.

title: Life in the Ancient Southwest
description: Explores the evidence of thousands of years of human cultural change that archaeologists have uncovered across the American Southwest. Ranges in time from the first appearance of humans to the time of Pueblo civilization.

title: Humanity and Global Environmental Change
description: Examines interaction between human populations and their environments. Explores relationships among population size, technology, climate, and behavior in various living societies worldwide. Particular attention to current environmental problems.

title: Ancient Hawaii
description: Covers the origins of traditional Hawaiian society as known through archaeology, historical documents, and oral history, as well the history of Hawaii from European contact to statehood.

title: East Asia in Motion
description: Anthropological examination of East Asia, focusing on China, Korea, and Japan. Topics include the family, economics, popular culture, and the body. Focus on processes of cultural transformation and the ways globalization, economic transformations, and political events affected change.

title: Rites of Passage: Anthropological Perspectives
description: Students study rites of passage across cultures and their meaning for human adaptation and flourishing, as well as experience their own rite of passage in guided lab work using anthropological methods.

title: Andean Archaeology
description: Archaeological exploration of ancient Andean civilizations, examining Indigenous societies from early settlement to the Inca Empire and Spanish invasion, emphasizing environment, political systems, religion, and long-term cultural continuity in South America.

title: Regulating Reproduction: Morality, Politics, (In)justice
description: Reproduction - the process that fuses individual bodies to the body politic - is a key site for processes of governance. Drawing on ethnographic research, film, and media, this course considers global reproductive politics regarding pregnancy, birth, abortion, embryo adoption, and other topics.

title: Gender, Violence, and Health
description: Examines how gender-based violence shapes individual subjective and collective experiences, material realities, and psychological states, as well as the impacts of interventions on intimate, interpersonal, local, and global scales.

title: Contesting Development: Global and Local Impacts and Human Rights
description: Critiques and discusses the impact of “economic development,” within a capitalist/globalization framework, on people’s lives and communities across the developing world. Examines how capitalist development poses challenges to human rights, and debates various political and economic positions on the causes, human impacts, and possible solutions to those challenges. Impacts including hunger, poverty, environmental degradation, global warming, spread of new diseases, ethnic conflict and ethnocide, terrorism, and religious fundamentalism are discussed. Also examines and debates possible alternative forms of development and modernization.

title: The Immigrant Experience
description: Explores the historical, social, cultural, and political dimensions of the U.S. immigrant experience and Americans’ attitudes toward immigrants. Examines issues such as bilingual education and illegal immigration.

title: Fantastic Archaeology and Pseudoscience: Lost Tribes, Sunken Continents, and Ancient Astronauts
description: Investigates various claims (e.g., ancient astronauts have visited Earth, archaeologists are not revealing secrets about the Maya calendar, and creation theory is a scientific alternative to the theory of human evolution) and how archaeologists respond to them.

title: Gender and Globalization: Cultural and Ethical Issues
description: An analysis of the impact of globalizing forces on women’s lives and identities, as well as on patterns of gender relations and ideology in various cultures around the world.

title: Economic Anthropology
description: How does technology shape a society's economy and culture? What do transactions tell us about cultural values? This course investigates the relationship between economics and culture across diverse societies.

title: Cultural Aspects of Business
description: Explores the cultural aspects of business and entrepreneurship at home and abroad. Also, addresses the relationship between anthropology and business, examining business in a holistic context.

title: Introduction to Ethnographic Methods
description: Introduces the methods and tools of ethnographic research. Relevant for students from a variety of disciplines. Topics include how to ask a research question, the conceptual work behind research, writing a research proposal, observation methods, interview techniques, data coding, ethnographic writing, and visual methods.

title: Culture and Diversity in American Life
description: An overview of contemporary U.S. culture, with an emphasis on how diversity (e.g., ethnicity, class, religion, and gender) is expressed in communities, in regions, and in the nation.

title: Health as a Human Right
description: Examines the concept of human rights critically, with an eye for cross-cultural variation and a particular focus on health-related rights.

title: Good Eats: Culture, Food, and the Global Grocery Market
description: Offers bio-cultural perspective on food that blends biological and medical information about human nutrition and development with an exploration of the global markets and cultures of eating.

title: Forensic Anthropology: Lessons Taught by Bones
description: Introduction to the identification of human remains, including conditions of preservation and decay. Estimating sex, stature, age, and ethnicity. Identifying pathology, trauma, and other causes of death.

title: Indians of North America
description: A survey of American-Indian and Eskimo life, past and present, with emphasis on the interaction of Indians and whites since 1492 and on contemporary American-Indian problems and enterprises: reservation and urban life, gambling, health care, and legal rights.

title: Latin America: Peoples, Places, and Power
description: Examines the development of Latin America in the context of global transformations since the 16th century. Special attention is given to the interaction of local communities with regional, national, and international systems of power.

title: Society and Culture in Contemporary Europe
description: Anthropological survey of social and cultural dimensions of contemporary European society. Explores unity and diversity within the region, and the role of gender, religion, class, ethnicity, and nationalism in structuring the lives of Europeans.

title: From Gold to Gambling: Native Americans of the Southwest
description: Introduction to the non-Pueblo and Pueblo peoples of the Greater Southwest, with a focus on Indian-Indian and Indian-EuroAmerican relations and the resultant transformations. Topics include the clash of cultures, tourism, gambling, legal rights, and urbanism.

title: Peoples and Cultures of the Middle East
description: This course employs the lens of cultural anthropology to explore the social, cultural, familial, religious, and political lives of Middle Easterners from a wide variety of countries and backgrounds.

title: Language in Culture and Society
description: An investigation of social and cultural factors affecting the use of language. Topics include linguistic variation, black English, women’s language, and body language.

title: Science and Technology in an Anthropological Perspective
description: Anthropological study of science and technology. Focuses on science as a form of knowledge and the impact of technology.

title: Magic, Myth, and Religion Across Cultures
description: A cross-cultural and comparative exploration of religion, ritual, magic, and supernatural belief systems. Examines how religion permeates other aspects of society and culture.

title: Global Urbanism: Implosions/Explosions
description: An introduction to urban life and culture around the world, including how to study cities, who inhabits cities, and the special features of city places and spaces.

title: Fire on Earth: An Introduction to Pyrogeography
description: Fire has been a transformative process in Earth's history. Today, fire threatens homes and lives on every continent. This course explores the varied roles of fire on Earth.

title: Living with Fire: Past, Present, Future
description: Explores the historical and contemporary challenges of living with wildfires.

title: Cultures and Environments of the Southwest
description: Patterns of land and resource use in prehistoric and early historic times in the Southwest. The focus is on the mutual influence of cultures and resources in the northern Rio Grande region.

title: Paradise Lost? Long-Term Perspectives on Human Impacts on the Environment
description: Using interdisciplinary archaeological, anthropological, and historical case studies from around the world, this course provides detailed examinations of human impacts on the environment over the last 400,000 years.

title: Sustainable Living: An Introduction to Systems and Resilience Thinking
description: Contemporary sustainability depends on an appreciation for the complex interactions between systems of people and nature. Introduces students to systems and resilience thinking to approach contemporary sustainability problems in new ways.

title: Unlikely Connections: Introduction to Human-Animal Interactions Past and Present
description: Introductory course on the new interdisciplinary science of anthrozoology, which takes the position that humans and animals have shared coevolutionary history spanning thousands of years.

title: Warfare and Violence: The Anthropology and Ethics of Human Conflict
description: An examination of the origins and development of human aggression, violence, and warfare using interdisciplinary data and theories from prehistory, ethnology, history, and political science.

title: The Plundered Past: Archaeology's Challenges in the Modern World
description: Provides an interdisciplinary understanding of the importance societies place on knowing, preserving, and altering evidence of the past. Special emphasis is placed on archaeology's role in understanding and preserving the past.

title: In Search of Ice Age Americans
description: The peopling of America during the Ice Age, reconstructed by various disciplines (e.g., archaeology, linguistics, and molecular biology), and what that reconstruction reveals about how people adapted to a truly new world.

description: Traces the theoretical developments in ethnology and archaeology from 1960 to the present, with intense readings and a focus on the potential utility of theoretical coherence in the discipline.

title: Hunter-Gatherers from Past and Present
description: Survey course of our common hunter-gatherer heritage from the prehistoric record through modern times. Focuses on how understanding hunter-gatherers can inform us about our current lifeways.

title: Introduction to Osteology I: Human-Animal Interactions
description: Explores the evolution of human and animal interactions through a comparative study and analysis of their skeletons. Examines variations in nature’s grand design, including the origins of different skeletal features, the evolution of these features over time, and the ways humans influenced the development of many of these features through processes such as targeted hunting and selective breeding. Introduces the science of taphonomy in hands-on learning labs. Students learn how isotopic and biomolecular analyses of animal skeletal remains help in understanding human–animal interactions.

description: Examines theories, practices of, and research on resilience. Students apply ethnographic methodologies to understand human responses to contemporary health challenges and as a mode of ethical care.

description: Examines the epistemology and history of biomedicine, medical bureaucracy, professionalism, medical education, alternative and popular medicine, economics, and health care.

description: Emphasizes cultural, artistic, and intellectual trends.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in ARBC 2402 or permission of instructor.

title: Advanced Arabic Conversation
description: Study of themes related to the Arabic experience. Primarily oriented toward conversation on topics of everyday life.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in ARBC 2302, or permission of the instructor.

title: Advanced Media Arabic
description: Introduces authentic texts and audio files from a wide variety of media sources and emphasizes the semantic and stylistic aspects of media Arabic rather than its grammar.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: ARBC 3301 and ARBC 3302, or placement test, or departmental permission.

title: Special Topics in Arabic
description: Independent study in Arabic language, literature, and culture in selected topics, authors, and genres.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ARBC 3302 or permission of instructor.

title: Special Topics in Arabic Literature and Culture
description: Independent study of selected topics, authors, and genres in Arabic literature and culture.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ARBC 3302 or permission of instructor.

title: Beginning American Sign Language I
description: An introductory study of grammar and language, with an emphasis on developing question-and-answer skills. The student learns conversational strategies to help maintain a conversation. Enrollment permission from the Second Language Adviser is required to enroll.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Restricted to students who have no prior ASL experience or have been placed into ASL 1401 by the ASL placement exam.

title: Beginning American Sign Language II
description: Examines the development of receptive and expressive language skills. Students learn to express, negotiate, and interpret meaning in American Sign Language. Students meeting these requirements will be able to enroll. Otherwise, approval from the WLL adviser is required for enrollment.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in ASL 1401 or the appropriate placement exam score.

title: American Sign Language II with Review
description: Reviews ASL fundamentals and increases student proficiency. This course continues to focus on the development of receptive and expressive ability with increasingly complex vocabulary, increased fingerspelling, and numbers fluency and accuracy. Approval from the WLL adviser is required for enrollment.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Restricted to students who have previous ASL experience but did not place into ASL 1402.

title: Intermediate American Sign Language I
description: Students improve receptive and expressive fluency while reinforcing appropriate grammar usage and conversation skills. Introduces deaf idioms and their use within Deaf culture.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in ASL 1402 or ASL 1502, or appropriate placement exam score.

title: ASL Fingerspelling and Numbers
description: Overview of basic fingerspelling techniques to improve receptive and expressive fingerspelling skills. Receptive skills emphasize whole-word and phrase recognition as well as identifying fingerspelling words in context. Expressive skills concentrate on the development of speed; clarity; and fluency of fingerspelled words, loan signs, and numbers.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Completion of ASL 2301 with a minimum grade of C-.

title: Introductory Biology Lab
description: Standard laboratory techniques are utilized to study living organisms, with an emphasis on cells as the components of life. One 3-hour laboratory each week.
prerequisites: Corequisite: BIOL 1301.

title: Introductory Biology Lab
description: A practical study of the diversity of living organisms with respect to anatomy, ecology, and evolution. One 3-hour laboratory each week.
prerequisites: Corequisite: BIOL 1302.

title: Biology for Liberal Arts
description: An introduction to the major concepts of biological thought for the nonscience major. Includes the equivalent of one laboratory session per week. BIOL 1300 is not open to students with prior credit in BIOL 1301 or BIOL 1401.

title: Introductory Biology
description: Introduction to the study of living organisms: basic organic chemistry of macromolecules, cellular energy, the cell and signaling pathways, cell division, Mendelian genetics, nucleic acids and gene expression. BIOL 1301/1101 and BIOL 1302/1102 are prerequisites to all advanced courses in biological sciences.
prerequisites: Prerequisite or corequisite: BIOL 1101.

title: Introductory Biology
description: Introduction to the study of living organisms: ecology, evolution, diversity, and physiology. BIOL 1301/1101 and BIOL 1302/1102 are prerequisites to all advanced courses in biological sciences.
prerequisites: Prerequisite or corequisite: BIOL 1102.

title: Nature and our Role in It
description: Explores the ecological roles of organisms, the ecological impact of human activity, and our role in building a sustainable future. Taught at SMU-in-Taos, New Mexico.

title: The Natural Environment
description: An introduction to major environments and their resident populations for the nonscience major. Includes the equivalent of one laboratory session each week. BIOL 1305 is not open to students with prior credit in BIOL 1302. (SMU-in-Taos)

title: Plant Biology
description: An introduction to the economic, social, and industrial aspects of plant substances and material for the nonscience major. Includes the equivalent of one laboratory session each week. BIOL 1308 is not open to students who have prior credit in BIOL 1302. (SMU-in-Taos)

title: Aquatic Biology of the American Southwest
description: For the nonscience major. Introduces the biology of lakes and streams in the American Southwest. Lectures and labs are conducted at Fort Burgwin, New Mexico. (SMU-in-Taos)

title: Introductory Undergraduate Research
description: A minimum of 5 hours per week doing supervised laboratory research. Offered on a pass/fail basis only. May be repeated twice for credit.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: At least sophomore standing, grade of C- or better in BIOL 1301/BIOL 1101 and BIOL 1302/BIOL 1102, and consent of instructor.
repeatability: May be repeated twice for credit.

title: Introductory Research II
description: A minimum of 5 hours per week doing supervised laboratory research. Offered on a pass/fail basis only. May be repeated twice for credit.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: BIOL 2101 and consent of instructor.
repeatability: May be repeated twice for credit.

title: Internship in Biology
description: Laboratory or fieldwork in biology at an on- or off-campus location. Pass/Fail only.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Departmental approval required.

title: Human Anatomy and Physiology I with Laboratory
description: The first part of a two-course sequence, this course covers a systemic approach to the study of the human body with a focus on the anatomical structure and function of the human neuromusculoskeletal systems and is offered for students pursuing PA, PT, and other allied health professions. This is the gateway course for the applied physiology and health management (APHM) major; successful completion is mandatory for admission to the APHM program, an approved STEM major. This course does not satisfy requirements for a biology major or minor, nor can it substitute for an advanced biology course in a program where one is required. To meet the requirements of most allied health professional programs, including PA and PT, students pursuing a graduate professional path are strongly encouraged to complete a full year of introductory biology courses (BIOL 1301/BIOL 1101 and BIOL 1302/BIOL 1102) with a grade of C or better. Some PA programs require a grade of B or better; therefore, it is important to review program specific requirements. Students may not receive credit for both APSM 2441 and BIOL 2441. Lab fee: $30.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Restricted to students who have fewer than 90 credit hours or have the instructor’s approval.

title: Human Anatomy and Physiology II with Laboratory
description: The second part of a two-course sequence, this course examines the gross anatomy and physiology of the endocrine, cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive, and urinary systems, their relationship with human health and performance, and is offered for students pursuing PA, PT, and other allied health professions. This course does not satisfy requirements for a biology major or minor, nor can it substitute for an advanced biology course in a program where one is required. To meet the requirements of most allied health professional programs, including PA and PT, students pursuing a graduate professional path are strongly encouraged to complete a full year of introductory biology courses (BIOL 1301/BIOL 1101 and BIOL 1302/BIOL 1102) with a grade of C or better. Some PA programs require a grade of B or better; therefore, it is important to review program specific requirements. Students may not receive credit for both APSM 2442 and BIOL 2442. Lab fee: $30.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: BIOL 2441.

title: Special Topics Abroad
description: Courses offered in SMU-approved international programs. May be repeated for credit under a different subtitle. A maximum of 6 hours of special topics abroad may be applied toward the B.A. or B.S. degree in biology. May not be applied toward the minor in biology.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Departmental approval.
repeatability: May be repeated for credit under a different subtitle.

title: Physiology Laboratory
description: Uses live organisms to study homeostasis and the following: cell cycle, cardiovascular, nervous, sensory, digestive, and respiratory physiology. Covers Latin and Greek stem words to reinforce medical terminology.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 3304 and BIOL 3350. Prerequisite or corequisite: BIOL 4306.

title: Molecular Genetics Laboratory
description: Students gain experience in investigative methods used in modern medical research, molecular biology, genetics, bioinformatics, forensic science, and the pharmaceutical and biotechnology industries.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 3304.

title: Microbiology Laboratory
description: Introduces microbiological methods for: inoculation of bacteria using aseptic technique, isolating bacterial colonies, identification of bacterial morphology using microscopy, enumeration and identification of bacteria using culture methods and differential media. One 3-hour lab each week.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: BIOL 1301/BIOL 1101, BIOL 1302/BIOL 1102 and C- or better in BIOL 3304 and BIOL 3350. Prerequisite or corequisite: BIOL 4376.

title: Special Topics Abroad
description: Courses offered in SMU-approved international programs. May be repeated for credit under a different subtitle. A maximum of 6 hours of special topics abroad may be applied toward the B.A. or B.S. degree in biology. May not be applied toward the minor in biology.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Departmental approval.
repeatability: May be repeated for credit under a different subtitle.

title: Evolution
description: A study of the principles of biological evolution. Includes natural selection, adaptation, molecular evolution, the formation of new species, the fossil record, biogeography, and principles of classification. Includes 3 hours of lecture each week.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: BIOL 1301/BIOL 1101 and C- or better in BIOL 3304.

title: Genetics
description: An introduction to the structure, function, and transmission of the hereditary material. Includes 3 hours of lecture each week.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 1301/BIOL 1101 and CHEM 1304.

title: Limnology: Aquatic Biology
description: The study of inland waters, integrating chemistry, physics, and biology. Emphasis is on identifying organisms and studying their interactions with the environment. Includes 2 hours of lecture and one 3-hour laboratory each week.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: BIOL 1301/BIOL 1101, BIOL 1302/BIOL 1102, and CHEM 1303.

title: Ecology
description: Basic principles and concepts of ecology, with emphasis on population and community interactions. Includes 3 hours of lecture each week.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: BIOL 1301/BIOL 1101, BIOL 1302/BIOL 1102; or permission of instructor.

title: Biology of Marine Mammals
description: A comparative study of marine mammal anatomy, morphology, physiology, life history and behavior, and adaptation to marine existence. Includes study of the effect of human activities on marine mammals, with special reference to northern European waters. (SMU-in-Copenhagen only)
prerequisites: Prerequisites: BIOL 1301/BIOL 1101, BIOL 1302/BIOL 1102, and CHEM 1303/CHEM 1113.

title: Wildlife Ecology
description: Ecological principles of ecosystems. Examines factors underlying distributions, population biology, co-evolution, and behavioral ecology, along with competition and predation, using examples from field studies. (SMU Abroad only)
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 3304 and BIOL 3350.

title: Biology of the Brain
description: Reviews the basic functioning of the brain and provides a deeper understanding of how people sense and interact with their environment.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: BIOL 1301/BIOL 1101, BIOL 1302/BIOL 1102.

title: Field Botany
description: Identification of vascular plants, with emphasis on ecological indicators. Lectures and laboratories conducted at Fort Burgwin, New Mexico, site of SMU-in-Taos.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: BIOL 1301/BIOL 1101, BIOL 1302/BIOL 1102.

title: Systematic Botany
description: An introduction to the history, nomenclature, family characteristics, identification, and biosystematics of the flowering plants. Lecture and laboratory work conducted at Fort Burgwin, New Mexico.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: BIOL 1301/BIOL 1101, BIOL 1302/BIOL 1102.

title: Cell Biology
description: The structure and function of cells. Includes 3 hours of lecture each week.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: BIOL 1301/BIOL 1101, BIOL 1302/BIOL 1102, and CHEM 1304.

title: Cancer Biology
description: Emphasis on the molecular features of oncogenesis and human cancers, including carcinogenesis, metastasis, and roles of genetic mutations and chromosomal aberrations during neoplasia.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 3350.

title: Paleobiology
description: A survey of biological diversity, phylogenetic analysis, rates of evolution, extinction, biogeography, taphonomy, and paleoecology.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in one of the following: BIOL 1301/BIOL 1101, BIOL 1302/BIOL 1102, or one 1300-level course in Earth sciences.

title: Internship in Biology
description: Biological research at an institution other than SMU. Credit does not apply toward the degree requirement for two laboratory classes. A student may only take one of the research courses for a letter grade: BIOL 3385, BIOL 3398, or Biol 4398. Prior departmental approval required.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 3304 and BIOL 3350.

title: Undergraduate Research I
description: A minimum of 9 hours per week doing research in the laboratory of a faculty member. Credit for this course does not apply toward the degree requirement for two laboratory courses. A student may only take one of the research courses for a letter grade: BIOL 3385, BIOL 3398, or Biol 4398.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Junior standing, C- or better in BIOL 3304 and BIOL 3350, and approval of faculty sponsor and the Undergraduate Studies Committee of the department.

title: Undergraduate Research II
description: Pass/fail only. Cannot be applied toward the requirements for the major in biological sciences.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C or better in BIOL 3398 and approval by the faculty sponsor and the Undergraduate Studies Committee of the department.

title: Genomics Lab
description: Covers genomic analysis pipelines from nucleic acid isolation to sequence analysis in Linux and R environments. Students independently design and execute a high-throughput sequencing experiment to measure genetic variation in natural populations. Withdrawal from BIOL 4305 requires withdrawal from BIOL 4105.
prerequisites: Prerequisite or corequisite: BIOL 4305; or permission of instructor.

title: Biological Chemistry Laboratory
description: An introduction to experiments commonly used in biochemical research. Students learn to perform experiments, analyze experimental data, and keep laboratory notebooks. One 3-hour lab per week. If CHEM 4110 is counted toward a chemistry major or minor, it cannot be counted toward a biological sciences major or minor.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 1301/BIOL 1101, BIOL 1302/BIOL 1102. Prerequisite or corequisite: BIOL 4310/CHEM 4310.

title: Immunobiology Laboratory
description: Provides experience in experimental techniques and strategies used in immunobiology labs, including cell culture, quantitative plate-based assays, and fluorescence-activated cell sorting. Two 3-hour labs each week for half a term.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: BIOL 3304, BIOL 3350. Prerequisite or corequisite: BIOL 4319.

title: Senior Seminar
description: Discussion of current problems of biological interest, 1 hour each week.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Senior standing; major in biology.

title: Bioethics Seminar
description: Discussion of current ethical issues in Biology.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 3304 and BIOL 3350. Restricted to biology, biochemistry, chemistry, or physics majors only.

title: Functional Anatomy and Histology Laboratory
description: A scientific study of Mammalian Anatomy, from the cellular level (Histology) through organ systems (dissections), including pathology cases and application of weekly vocabulary lists of Latin and Greek stem words. Withdrawal from BIOL 4306 or BIOL 4364 requires withdrawal from BIOL 4164.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 3304 and BIOL 3350. Prerequisite or corequisite: BIOL 4306 or BIOL 4364.

title: Gene Editing Lab
description: A project-based lab course in which students use CRISPR-Cas9 to edit genes in model organisms and learn to design gene editing experiments. Must be taken with the lecture component BIOL 4380. Withdrawal from BIOL 4380 requires withdrawal from BIOL 4180. Non-honors students may enroll with the permission of the instructor and the department if they possess competence in basic laboratory research techniques.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 3304 and BIOL 3350. Corequisite: BIOL 4380. Restricted to Honors students.

title: Genomics and Bioinformatics
description: Impact of completely sequenced genomes on current experimental and computational approaches to biomedical research. Introduction to the technology, biology, and software exploited by molecular biology, genealogy, and medical diagnostic labs.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 3304 and junior standing.

title: Human Anatomy with Physiology
description: Explores human anatomy and physiology, with an emphasis on cellular mechanisms that influence organ system functions. Covers nervous, cardiovascular, respiratory, and renal systems. Also covers abnormal anatomy and physiology (pathology), where appropriate, as part of clinical case studies.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 3304, BIOL 3350; CHEM 1113, CHEM 1114, CHEM 1303, CHEM 1304.

title: Biological Chemistry: Macromolecular Structure and Function
description: Introduces the structure and function of macromolecules of biological importance, with a focus on nucleic acid and protein structure, enzyme kinetics, and carbohydrate and lipid chemistry. Includes 3 hours of lecture each week. The accompanying laboratory (BIOL 4110) is strongly recommended for biology majors. If CHEM 4310 is counted towards a chemistry major or minor, it cannot be counted towards a biological sciences major or minor.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in CHEM 3371, CHEM 3372 and junior standing.

title: Biological Chemistry:  Metabolism
description: Introduction to the pathways and regulatory events in the metabolism of carbohydrates, lipids, amino acids, and nucleotides. Includes 3 hours of lecture each week. If CHEM 4311 is counted toward a chemistry major or minor, it cannot be counted toward a biological sciences major or minor.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: BIOL 1301/BIOL 1101, BIOL 1302/BIOL 1102, and CHEM 3372.

title: Immunobiology
description: Introduction to fundamental concepts of the immune system.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 3304 and BIOL 3350.

title: Molecular Biology: Control and Expression of Genetic Information
description: DNA structure and replication, control of transcription and translation, and techniques in molecular genetics and recombinant DNA technology.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 3304 and CHEM 3372.

title: Molecular Biology of Eukaryotes
description: Structure and function of eukaryotic chromosomes as mediators of gene expression during growth, differentiation, and oncogenesis. A student cannot have previously completed BIOL 4320.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: BIOL 3304, CHEM 3372; and junior standing.

title: General and Molecular Virology
description: Emphasis on the molecular aspects of viral replication and pathogenesis, including the roles of viruses in emerging human infectious diseases, cancer, and bioterrorism.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 3304 and junior standing.

title: Developmental Biology
description: Developmental processes in animals. Includes 3 hours of lecture each week.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: BIOL 1301/BIOL 1101, BIOL 1302/BIOL 1102, and C- or better in BIOL 3304.

title: Clinical Neurobiology
description: Covers the structure and function of the nervous system under physiological and pathological conditions along with bioethics in neurobiology research. An emphasis on cellular mechanisms illustrates the links between neuropathology and neurological and psychiatric disorders.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 3304 and BIOL 3350; CHEM 1113, CHEM 1114, CHEM 1303, and CHEM 1304.

title: Neuroimmunology
description: Explores how immune cells influence the central and peripheral nervous systems. Topics include neuroinflammation, repair mechanisms, and immunity’s role in maintaining health and contributing to neurodegenerative diseases.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in one of the following: BIOL 4319, BIOL 4333, or BIOL 4364; and consent of instructor.

title: Molecular Basis of Brain Development and Degeneration
description: Covers the molecular biology of brain development and degeneration. Interactive course that includes lectures and student presentations of publications describing important research findings related to neurodevelopment and neurodegeneration.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 3304 and BIOL 3350.

title: Integrated Human Physiology with Endocrinology
description: Normal function and diseases of the major hormone systems of the body including the hypothalamus/pituitary axes; the thyroid gland; reproduction and sexual development; digestion and metabolism including the pancreas, bone, and calcium metabolism; and the adrenal glands.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 3304 and BIOL 3350.

title: Biotechnology and Nanotechnology
description: Introduction to current techniques and emerging applications of biotechnology and nanobiotechnology in medicine, agriculture, forensic and aquatic sciences, and bioremediation.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 3304 and CHEM 3371.

title: Microbiology
description: The biology of microorganisms, with an emphasis on diversity, disease, and the environment. Includes 3 hours of lecture each week.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 3304 and BIOL 3350.

title: Gene Editing: CRISPR
description: Explores CRISPR-based gene editing technologies and their use in treating genetic diseases. Draws extensively from scientific literature to give students insights into modern biotechnology applications.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 3304 and BIOL 3350.

title: Physical Chemistry of Proteins
description: Fundamental aspects of techniques used to interrogate the thermodynamics and kinetics of protein conformational changes, with emphasis on atomic resolution structural techniques.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: BIOL 4310/CHEM 4310, CHEM 4383 and CHEM 4384, and instructor approval.

title: Honors Undergraduate Research I
description: For students in the departmental distinction program. A student may only take one of the research courses for a letter grade: BIOL 3385, BIOL 3398, or Biol 4398.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in BIOL 3304 and BIOL 3350, approval of faculty sponsor, and admission to departmental distinction program.

title: Honors Undergraduate Research II
description: Pass/fail only. Cannot be applied toward the requirements for the major in biological sciences. For students in the departmental distinction program.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: B+ or better in BIOL 4398.

title: General Chemistry Laboratory
description: One 3-hour laboratory period each week.
prerequisites: Prerequisite or corequisite: CHEM 1303.

title: General Chemistry Laboratory
description: One 3-hour laboratory period each week.
prerequisites: Prerequisites or corequisites: CHEM 1304 and CHEM 1113.

title: Chemistry for Liberal Arts
description: Introductory course in chemistry designed for non-majors. A background in chemistry is not needed. Topics include atoms, molecules, pollution, ozone, chemical reactions, electromagnetic radiation, energy, water, acids and bases, nuclear reactions, chemistry of nutrition, drugs, batteries, and polymers and plastics.

title: Preparatory Chemistry
description: For students desiring to strengthen their background in chemistry prior to enrolling in the general chemistry course CHEM 1303.

title: General Chemistry
description: Primarily for science majors, premed students, and engineering students. Introduces the fundamental principles and theories of chemistry, including stoichiometry, the structure of matter, energy relationships involved in the transformation of matter, the dynamics of such transformations, and some descriptive chemistry of the important elements. Withdrawal from CHEM 1303 requires withdrawal from CHEM 1113.
prerequisites: Prerequisite to all advanced courses in the department. Prerequisites: C- or higher in CHEM 1302, appropriate equivalent credit for CHEM 1303, or a passing grade on the Chemistry Placement Exam.

title: General Chemistry
description: Primarily for science majors, premed students, and engineering students. Continuation of the introduction to the fundamental principles and theories of chemistry. Topics include solution chemistry, kinetics, equilibrium, thermodynamics, electrochemistry, polymer chemistry, and organic chemistry. Withdrawal from CHEM 1304 requires withdrawal from CHEM 1114.
prerequisites: Prerequisite to all advanced courses in the department. Prerequisites: C- or higher in CHEM 1303.

title: Organic Chemistry Laboratory
description: One 3-hour laboratory period each week.
prerequisites: Prerequisite or corequisite: CHEM 3371.

title: Organic Chemistry Laboratory
description: One 3-hour laboratory period each week.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CHEM 3117. Prerequisite or corequisite: CHEM 3372.

title: Quantitative Analysis
description: Involves the theory and practice of quantitative analytical chemistry techniques, including gravimetric, volumetric, electrochemical, and spectroscopic analyses. Includes 3 hours of lecture and two 4 hour laboratory periods per week for one-half term.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or higher in CHEM 1303, CHEM 1304, CHEM 1113, CHEM 1114.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: Designed to satisfy the requirements of the chemistry major and health-related professions student. The first term deals primarily with aliphatic chemistry, with special emphasis on stereochemistry. The second term emphasizes aromatic substances and the chemistry of biologically relevant molecules.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or higher in CHEM 1303, CHEM 1113, CHEM 1304, CHEM 1114.

title: Organic Chemistry
description: For chemistry majors and students interested in health-related professions. Emphasizes spectroscopy and the chemistry of functional groups.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or higher in CHEM 3371.

title: Undergraduate Research
description: For students who hold research fellowships but are not enrolled in any credit hour courses. No tuition.

title: Biological Chemistry Laboratory
description: One 3-hour laboratory period each week. If CHEM 4110 is counted toward a chemistry major or minor, it cannot be counted toward a biological sciences major or minor.
prerequisites: Corequisite: CHEM 4310.

title: Laboratory Methods in Physical Chemistry
description: Laboratory experiments with emphasis on thermodynamics, chemical kinetics, and physical biochemistry. Includes a half-hour of lecture and 5 hour laboratory period each week for 5 weeks.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CHEM 4383.

title: Advanced Physical Chemistry Laboratory
description: Laboratory experiments with emphasis on chemical kinetics and molecular spectroscopy. Includes a half-hour of lecture and 5 hour laboratory period each week for 5 weeks.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CHEM 4187. Corequisite: CHEM 4384 or permission of instructor.

title: Inorganic Synthesis Laboratory
description: Introduces advanced techniques and methods used in the synthesis of inorganic compounds.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Permission of instructor.

title: Introduction to Computational Chemistry
description: Besides the normal lab experiments, modern chemists and biochemists perform “experiments” on the computer by calculating the outcome of chemical and/or biochemical reactions. Introduces this new field in a hands-on fashion, and uses major quantum chemical packages. Note: Class assignments and projects are completed in the computer lab outside of the regularly scheduled class times.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: CHEM 1303, CHEM 1304 or permission of instructor.

title: Special Topics in Chemistry
description: Presentation of advanced special topics in chemistry that are at the forefront of current chemical interest. Content varies from term to term.

title: Biological Chemistry: Macromolecular Structure and Function
description: Introduces the structure and function of macromolecules of biological importance, with a focus on nucleic acid and protein structure, enzyme kinetics, and carbohydrate and lipid chemistry. Includes 3 hours of lecture each week. The accompanying laboratory (CHEM 4110) is strongly recommended for chemistry majors. If CHEM 4310 is counted toward a chemistry major or minor, it cannot be counted toward a biological sciences major or minor.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in CHEM 3371, CHEM 3372 and junior standing.

title: Biological Chemistry: Metabolism
description: Introduction to the pathways and regulatory events in the metabolism of carbohydrates, lipids, amino acids, and nucleotides. Includes 3 hours of lecture per week.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: CHEM 3371, CHEM 3372.

title: Modern Physical Organic Chemistry
description: Covers advanced topics in organic chemistry including molecular orbital theory, organometallic mechanisms, and photochemistry. Emphasis is placed on using mechanistic understanding to predict chemical reactivity.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: CHEM 1303, CHEM 1304, CHEM 3371, and CHEM 3372.

title: Medicinal Chemistry
description: Highlights the close relationships of organic chemistry and biochemistry with the field of medicine. Relies on the departmental computational laboratory to permit three-dimensional visualization of molecular interactions. Includes 3 hours of lecture each week.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: CHEM 3371, CHEM 3372.

title: Introduction to Polymer Chemistry
description: This course provides basic information on the synthesis, physical properties, and solution properties of high molecular weight molecules. Plastics, manufacturing, and fabrication of polymers are discussed.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: CHEM 3371 and CHEM 3372.

title: Introduction to Molecular Modeling and Computer-Assisted Drug Design
description: Presents a thorough and in-depth overview of methods and techniques in computer-assisted drug design. Topics include drug discovery and drug design, molecular recognition and docking, ligand-receptor interactions, pharmacophore searching, virtual screening, de novo design, molecular graphics, and chemometrics. Note: Class assignments and projects are completed in the computer lab outside of the regularly scheduled class times.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: CHEM 1303, CHEM 1304 or permission of instructor.

title: Understanding Chemistry
description: Focuses on a general understanding of chemistry in terms of models and concepts that describe structure, stability, reactivity, and other properties of molecules in a simple, yet very effective way.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: CHEM 1303, CHEM 1304 or permission of instructor.

title: Introduction to Nanotechnology
description: Introduces nanotechnology, which is expected to change lives and society more than computer technology and electricity have done together. Discusses nanomaterials and their applications.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: CHEM 1303, CHEM 1304 or permission of instructor.

title: Physical Chemistry of Proteins
description: Discusses the fundamental aspects of techniques used to interrogate the thermodynamics and kinetics of protein conformational changes, with emphasis on atomic resolution structural techniques.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: CHEM 4383 and CHEM 4384, knowledge of basic biochemistry, and permission of instructor.

title: Physical Chemistry I
description: Gas laws; kinetic molecular theory; introduction to thermodynamics, with applications to phase transitions and chemical equilibrium; chemical kinetics.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: CHEM 1114 and CHEM 1304 with a grade of C or better, PHYS 1105 and PHYS 1304 or PHYS 1308, and MATH 1337, or permission of instructor.

title: Physical Chemistry II
description: Elements of quantum mechanics and its description of many-electron atoms, bonding, and spectroscopy; intermolecular forces; structure of solids; and transport properties of fluids.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CHEM 4383.

title: Advanced Inorganic Chemistry
description: Survey of the bonding, structure, and reactivity of inorganic compounds. Also, coordination, organometallic, and main group element chemistry. Includes 3 hours of lecture each week. Recommended: CHEM 4384.

title: Advanced Organic Chemistry
description: Includes 3 hours of lecture each week.

title: Advanced Physical Chemistry

description: The theory, operation, and application of instrumentation used in the modern chemical laboratory. Includes 2 hours of lecture and two 3-hour laboratory periods each week.

title: SMU-UTSW Undergraduate Research Fellowship
description: Provides selected students (Fellows) with an opportunity to perform research at the UT Southwestern Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences under the guidance of UTSW faculty and an SMU faculty mentor. Fellows conduct this research full time for one semester on the UTSW campus while remaining full-time SMU students. Students are expected to carry out a well-defined research project and make original contributions to their scientific discipline. The SMU faculty mentor assigns the final grade which includes an evaluation from the UTSW faculty member, a mid-term research paper, and a final research poster presentation. A minimum overall GPA in the major of 3.25.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or higher in CHEM 1303, CHEM 1113, CHEM 1304, CHEM 1114, CHEM 3371, CHEM 3117, CHEM 3372, and CHEM 3118.

title: Beginning Chinese
description: Introduction to spoken and written Mandarin Chinese. Emphasizes intensive drills in sounds and tones, sentence structure, and a vocabulary of 500 characters. Students attend three weekly master classes plus 2 hours of practice in small groups. Computer, video, and audio assignments are required. Approval from the WLL adviser is required for enrollment.

Students attend three weekly master classes plus 2 hours of practice in small groups. Computer, video, and audio assignments are required. Students meeting these requirements will be able to enroll. description: Enhances basic language skills learned in beginning Chinese but focuses on language proficiency, particularly in the areas of description, narration, correspondence, and comparisons based on situational context. Students attend four weekly classes. Video and audio materials are used. Students meeting these requirements will be able to enroll. Otherwise, approval from the WLL adviser is required for enrollment.

title: Advanced Chinese
description: Emphasizes the refinement of skills in Mandarin Chinese through the study of selected topics in contemporary Chinese culture and society. Students develop the ability to express themselves in sustained oral and written forms.

title: Advanced Chinese, Second Term
description: Enhances students’ proficiency in Mandarin Chinese through a multimedia software program. Special concentration is given to China’s current affairs through the use of authentic journalistic materials: television news and newspaper reports.

title: Directed Studies in Chinese
description: Independent study in Chinese literature and culture in selected topics, authors, and genres. Permission of department required.

title: Readings in Chinese Literature and Culture
description: An upper-level course designed for students who have finished third-year Chinese. Students enhance their four language skills, especially reading and writing, through a wide variety of primary, unedited texts.

title: Chinese Culture and Society in Films
description: An advanced course for students who have completed CHIN 4381. Enhancement of all four language skills through unedited texts and films from China and Taiwan. Students may only take CHIN 4382 or WL 3312.

title: Myth and Thought in the Ancient World
description: Explores the conceptual and philosophical underpinnings of ancient understandings of reality in Western and non-Western cultures in both ancient and modern times. Materials for investigation will be primarily textual, including myths, epics, tragedies, and philosophical discourse in ancient Greece.

title: Dedman College Advanced Research
description: Independent research for students pursuing distinction in interdisciplinary or individualized majors or engaged in advanced independent research in relation to other Dedman College programs. Enrollment in this course requires preapproval of the senior associate dean of academic affairs.

Enrollment in this course requires preapproval of the senior associate dean of academic affairs.

title: A Practical Introduction to Data Science
description: Provides a first introduction to the exciting field of data science using applications and case studies from various domains (e.g., social media, marketing, sociology, engineering, digital humanities). Introduces data-centric thinking, including a discussion of how data is acquired, managed, manipulated, visualized, and used, to support problem-solving. The fundamental practical skills necessary are taught in class, and each step is illustrated with small examples. Tools presented in this course include SQL and Excel, along with other state-of-the-art tools. No prior knowledge of statistics, math, or programming is necessary.

title: An Introduction to Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning Methodology in the Social Sciences
description: Provides students with foundational tools that enable them to effectively deploy quantitative methods built around Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning methodology in social science contexts, in particular, in more advanced courses in the social sciences. The city of Dallas and Dallas County provide the data laboratory in which these tools are introduced. Students gain facility in the R programming language by modifying a suite of codes that analyze census data, voter data, flight data (DFW and Love Field), and city budget data.

title: Principles of Microeconomics: Consumers, Firms, and Markets
description: Explains tools of economic analysis and focuses on the individual participants in the economy: producers, workers, employers, and consumers.

title: Principles of Macroeconomics: Inflation, Recession, and Unemployment
description: Covers inflation, unemployment, and growth from both national and global perspectives. Tools of economic analysis include models of open economies.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in ECO 1311.

title: Intermediate Microeconomics
description: Building on topics covered in ECO 1311, this course considers problems of microeconomics that are more advanced, with a focus on understanding how consumers behave, firms make pricing and output decisions, and market structure impacts the behavior of firms and consumers.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 1311; ECO 1312; and MATH 1309, MATH 1337 or MATH 1408.

title: Intermediate Macroeconomics
description: Investigates the factors that influence the level of aggregate income in an economy and the decision-making that ultimately results in the determination of levels of consumption, investment, or employment. Students analyze the impact of various government fiscal policies (using general equilibrium models) and the behavior of business cycles and patterns across various countries.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 1311, ECO 1312, and ECO 3301.

title: Money and Banking
description: Analyzes central and commercial banking. Reserved for economics majors and markets and cultures majors only.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in ECO 1311, ECO 1312.

title: Internship in Economics
description: This advanced economics internship credit course requires weekly journal entries reflecting student experience. Approval from the director of undergraduate studies is required.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Reserved for economics majors only.

title: Internship in Economics II
description: This advanced economics internship credit course requires weekly journal entries reflecting student experience. Approval from the director of undergraduate studies is required.

title: Internship in Economics III
description: This advanced economics internship credit course requires weekly journal entries reflecting student experience. Approval from the director of undergraduate studies is required.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Reserved for economics majors only.

title: Topics
description: Topics vary. Repeating this course requires approval by the Director of Undergraduate Studies.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 3301; ECO 3302; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Economics of Human Rights
description: Investigates decision-making factors and economic theory related to human rights issues, specifically capital punishment, violence against women, seeking asylum, terrorism, child abuse, genocide, and hate.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in ECO 1311, ECO 1312, ECO 3301, ECO 3302; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: International Trade
description: Examines international trade in goods and services among countries and develops a framework for analyzing trade policy issues. The course covers only the real effects of trade and not international financial issues.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 3301; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Health Economics
description: An overview of how economic principles (scarcity, incentives, markets) are applied to health, healthcare, and health policy, covering topics like insurance, provider/consumer behavior, cost-effectiveness of interventions, government's role, and improving population health outcomes through economic analysis and modeling.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in ECO 3301; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Urban Economics
description: Applies economic concepts to an understanding of urban form; urban growth; trends in size and structure of urban areas; and the predominant urban public issues of transportation, housing, land-use planning, and environmental controls. Provides an opportunity to study particular topics in depth. Note: This course makes extensive use of calculus (MATH 1309/MATH 1337) and statistics (STAT 2331).
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 3301 and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Cultural Economics
description: Introduces the field of cultural economics, with a focus on welfare valuations, valuation of nonmarket goods, and intellectual property.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in ECO 3301; STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Strategic Behavior
description: Introduces the basic concepts and tools of game theory, with applications to various areas of economics. The various topics are unified by the techniques employed for determining the outcome in particular situations. Note: This course makes extensive use of calculus and statistics (STAT 2331).
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 3301; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Experimental and Behavioral Economics
description: Students study the field of behavioral economics in which the underlying assumptions of economics models are tested using experimental techniques. Guided by behavioral regularities, new models of behavior are introduced. Recommended: ECO 4341, ECO 4350.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in ECO 3301; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
description: Provides a basis for the modeling of decision-making under conditions of incomplete information. Note: This course makes extensive use of calculus and statistics (STAT 2331).
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 3301; ECO 3302; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Ethics in Economics
description: An explanation of historical and current perspectives of how societies and economies function.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in ECO 3301; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Introductory Econometrics
description: The basic concepts of econometrics and, in particular, regression analysis, with topics geared to first-time regression users.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 3301; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Labor Economics
description: An overview of labor supply and labor demand models, with extensions to models of taxes and tax credits, welfare, and Social Security. Also, models of wage determination and extensions such as the effects of minimum wage, performance-based pay, unions, and discrimination.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 3301; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Economics of the Family
description: An overview of the economic analysis of the family, covering topics such as household decision-making, marriage markets, fertility, and the impact of public policy on family structures.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in ECO 3301; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Law and Economics
description: Examines economic theories that explain the development of common law and constitutional law and the economic implications of contracts, antitrust laws, and liability rules.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 3301; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Economic and Business Forecasting
description: Presentation of methods used by economists to forecast economic and business trends and ways of evaluating the usefulness of these methods.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: STAT 2331 or STAT 4340; and ECO 4350.

title: Environmental Economics
description: Provides insights into why environmental damages and degradation arise, and how such market failures may be addressed.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in ECO 1311, ECO 1312, ECO 3301, ECO 3302; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Causal Inference in Economics
description: Presents a modern approach to answering causal questions in economics. Topics include: concepts of causality, potential outcomes, classical experiments, and tools of causal identification using observational data. Such tools include regression, stratification, matching, weighting, regression discontinuity, differences-in-differences, synthetic controls, and instrumental variables. Application of these methods to diverse topics in economics using statistical software is a large component of this course.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: STAT 2331 or STAT 4340; and ECO 4350.

title: International Macroeconomic Theory and Policy
description: Explores implications of contemporary banking and foreign exchange practices, with a focus on the macroeconomic interactions among national economies and international systematic adjustments expected from market disturbances and shifting government policies. Students evaluate the operation of the international monetary system from the gold-standard period to the present.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 3301; ECO 3302; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Economic Development: Macroeconomic Perspectives
description: A macroeconomic examination of the economic issues faced by developing countries. Topics include population growth, national savings, capital accumulation, human capital formation, government institutions, and international integration.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 3302; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Economics of Education
description: An economic analysis of the state of the U.S. educational system. Topics include trends in academic achievement, educational production functions, teacher labor markets, and educational reforms.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 3301; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Economic Growth
description: Examines the facts and theories of economic growth, the economics of technological changes, and the role of governments and markets in promoting or impeding economic development.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 3301; ECO 3302; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Political Economy
description: Explores the relationship between political institutions and economic development, covering key theoretical issues as well as recent empirical evidence. Recommended: ECO 4357.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 3301; ECO 3302; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Economics of National Security
description: Examines the multifaceted impact of global interdependence on nations and their economies, analyzing vulnerabilities nations face amid heightened interconnectedness through the intricate dynamics of global trade, finance, and diplomacy. Recommended: ECO 4363.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 3301; ECO 3302; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Public Finance
description: Develops principles to be used when evaluating a specific tax and uses them to investigate specific federal revenue sources such as taxes on personal and corporate income. Recommended: ECO 3302.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in ECO 3301; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Economics of Policy Design and Evaluation
description: Focuses on theoretical principles useful for analyzing the role of government intervention. Topics may vary from year to year.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C– or better in ECO 3301; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Foundations of Financial Economics
description: Applies the tools of economic analysis to financial decision-making. Emphasis is placed on developing a framework for understanding the problems and solutions associated with the economic nature of finance.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 3301, ECO 3355, ACCT 2301; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340. Restricted to economics majors and minors only.

title: Computing for Economics
description: Emphasis on learning computer programs commonly used in economics with the objective of teaching programming skills used in data discovery and summarization, graphics, file manipulation, iterative procedures, and simulations. Programs could include SAS, R, PYTHON, STATA, SPSS, MATLAB, and SQL.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in ECO 3301, ECO 3302, and ECO 4350; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Theory of Industrial Structure
description: A focus on the structure and behavior of firms in the marketplace. The course considers both the exercise of market power in relatively simple markets with a single firm as well as the more complicated exercise of market power in markets with multiple firms.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 3301; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Network Economics and Agent Based Models
description: Explores characteristics of networks and how our choices affect their structure and outcomes. Applications include diffusion (of ideas, fashion, or viruses), web rankings, information cascades, and market outcomes.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 3301; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Economic History and Development
description: Economic principles are used to explore important and controversial questions.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 3301; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Financial Economics and Investment Behavior
description: Gives a theoretical basis for financial analysis within the context of the total process of investment decision-making and develops the theoretical foundations for analysis of equities and bonds as well as portfolio performance. Reserved for economics majors and minors.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in ECO 3301, ECO 4368; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Economic Analysis I
description: Analysis of basic models of the firm under purely competitive markets and monopolistic competition and simple consumer behavior models. The exposition employs basic mathematical tools such as calculus.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 3301; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340. Restricted to Mathematical Economics, B.S. majors only, or to students with departmental consent from the Director of Undergraduate Studies.

title: Economic Analysis II
description: Course open only to BS Mathematical Economics majors only, or students with departmental consent from the Director of Undergraduate Studies.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 3301; ECO 3302; and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Macroeconomics: Theory and Policy
description: Examines new developments in the analysis of business cycles, the causes and consequences of inflation, and the sources of economic growth.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: C- or better in the following: ECO 3301, ECO 3302 and STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Independent Study in Economics
description: By arrangement with departmental director of undergraduate studies. Eligible students undertake a research paper under the supervision of the faculty sponsor and give an oral presentation of the paper. Note: This course can only be taken once.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: ECO 3301, ECO 3302, two advanced economics classes, 3.500 GPA in economics classes, and one of the following: STAT 2331 or STAT 4340.

title: Preparation for Departmental Honors Distinction Thesis
description: A research seminar in which selected students develop independent research projects under faculty supervision, culminating in a research proposal demonstrating mastery of economic reasoning and scholarly communication. The GPA requirement will be checked at enrollment time in March/April of the junior year.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Overall GPA of 3.5 or higher; completion of ECO 3302 and one of STAT 2331 or STAT 4340 with economics GPA of 3.7 or higher and no grade below B in ECO 3301 and ECO 3302; completion of at least two 4000-level economics field courses by start of fall semester (Mathematical Economics majors exempt from field course requirement); senior standing; admission by competitive summer application. Prerequisite or corequisite: ECO 4350.

title: Departmental Distinction in Economics
description: By arrangement with departmental director of undergraduate studies. Eligible students undertake a research paper under the supervision of a faculty sponsor and give an oral presentation of the paper.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Completion of ECO 4397 with a grade of B- or above, and instructor approval.

title: Foundations for Rhetoric
description: Writing paragraphs and short, analytic, thesis-directed essays in response to texts. Work on reading comprehension, principles of effective sentence construction, and punctuation.

title: Cultures of Medieval Chivalry
description: The development of the ideal of chivalry from its origins in the medieval legends of King Arthur to modern literature.

title: The World of Shakespeare
description: Introductory study of eight or nine of Shakespeare's important plays, placed in historical, intellectual, and cultural contexts.

title: The American Heroine
description: Images of the American heroine in popular and traditional literature, studied in terms of their reflection of the evolving roles of American women.

title: Speculative Fiction
description: An introductory study of selected 20th-century novels emphasizing both ideas of modernity and the historical or cultural contexts that generate these ideas.

title: Myths of the American West: Legend, Fact, and the Fictions of Conquest
description: Through literature, history and film, this course explores the multiple mythologies that have come to represent the idea of the West within American culture.

title: Literature of Minorities
description: Representative works of African-American, Asian-American, gay, Hispanic-American, and Native American literature, in their immediate cultural context and against the background of the larger American culture.

title: English Studies Abroad
description: SMU credit for English courses taken in University-approved programs abroad. Departmental consent required.

title: Introduction to Literature
description: An introduction to the study of literature including a range of literary genres and periods, varying by term.

title: Power, Passion, and Protest in British Literature
description: A survey of the history of British literature, from its medieval beginnings to the 20th century, with emphasis on literature as an instrument of power and desire.

title: Spreadsheet Literacy: Excel for Students in the Humanities and Natural and Social Sciences
description: An introduction to Excel as it is commonly used in the workplace. Students will learn to organize and analyze data, use and link worksheets, create tables and charts, and communicate results of their analyses in clear, readable prose.

title: Business Writing
description: Introduction to business and professional communication, including a variety of writing and speaking tasks, and the observation and practice of rhetorical strategies, discourse conventions, and ethical standards associated with workplace culture.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: WRTR 1312, WRTR 2303, or WRTR 2305.

title: Ethical Leadership and Language of Influence: Balancing Professionalism with Ethical Communication
description: This writing-intensive course explores ethical leadership through rhetorical analysis, discourse studies, and civic ethics. Students develop critical thinking, persuasive communication, and ethical reasoning skills through case studies, research, and professional writing while balancing professionalism and wellbeing.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: WRTR 1312, WRTR 2303, or WRTR 2305.

title: Imagination and Interpretation
description: An introduction to literary studies based on topics that vary from term to term. May be repeated twice for credit under a different subtitle.
repeatability: May be repeated twice for credit under a different subtitle.

title: Poetry
description: Analysis, interpretation, and appreciation of poetry, with attention to terms and issues relevant to the genre.

title: Fiction
description: Analysis, interpretation, and appreciation of fiction, with attention to terms and issues relevant to the genre.

title: Introduction to Literary Study
description: An introduction to the discipline for beginning English majors, covering methods of literary analysis in selected texts spanning a range of genres and historical periods.

description: Examines how technology can advance our understanding of language, literature, and culture. A hands-on introduction to applying cutting-edge technologies including text mining, digitization, metadata, and mapping to analyze literature.

description: A collaborative summer course with Shakespeare Dallas. Students closely study a Shakespeare play, write about it, attend a performance, and collaborate with the organization on publicity for the show.
